title: Crispin and the Shy Stars
markdown:
Crispin the squirrel, whose tail was like a gentle question mark always wondering what comes next, was full of a quiet eagerness. He had a nose that twitched at every interesting smell, and his little paws loved to dart and explore. Today his bright curious eyes were fixed on the sky, slowly turning from cheerful blue to a soft blushing pink. “Lark,” he whispered, a soft rustle like dry leaves on a breeze, “when will the stars come out? I do so wish to see them soon.” His paws twinkled beneath him as he swayed, wanting to bounce higher toward the sky. He was looking forward to the sparkly lights he’d heard so much about.

Lark the lamb, whose fleece was as soft and white as a brand-new cloud, lay beside a patch of sweet-smelling clover. She watched his gentle swaying with large calm eyes, her own tail giving a slow contented swish. “Now, Crispin,” she murmured, a low soft bleat like a quiet melody on a faraway flute, “the stars don’t just pop out like little fireflies. They take their time. They are shy little lights, and they wait for the deep quiet to feel brave enough to peek out from behind the sun’s bright curtain.” She gave a soft sigh, a whisper of warm milky air. “Waiting can be a sweet adventure all its own. A peaceful one.”

But Crispin’s thoughts fluttered like restless moths, all wanting to see the stars now. He scampered up a low branch of a wise old oak, its leaves whispering secrets to the wind, then twitched his nose and hopped down again, claws making a soft patter on the bark. He watched a wisp of dandelion fluff float by, imagining it a shooting star, and tried to count the last rays of sunshine as they stretched long and golden across the meadow. “An adventure is supposed to be exciting, Lark!” he called down, wondering if he was missing something wonderful. He wriggled his nose, a tiny thoughtful frown between his bright eyes.

Lark nestled a little deeper into the soft cool grass, pulling her cloud-like fleece closer. “Ah, but Crispin,” she murmured, like a stream finding its way over smooth stones, “the real adventure is noticing. It’s in the quiet moments. Watch how the sky changes from pink to purple, and then to a deep indigo, like a velvety blanket being pulled up. Listen to the crickets starting their evening lullaby. Feel the gentle breeze that whispers to the leaves, a soft caress on your fur. That is where the magic begins to unfold.” She closed her eyes a moment, breathing in twilight air, and when she opened them she saw a tiny shy twinkle near the edge of the sky, just above the rolling hills. “Oh, look. The first one is here. See?”

Crispin paused his twitching. He stopped watching the fading light and looked up, following Lark’s soft gaze. A single tiny point of light glimmered, like a diamond spilled from a giant’s pocket. Then another, and another, softly blinking, little scattered jewels on a vast darkening velvet cloth. He sat down right beside her, his tail no longer questioning but resting gently, curled around him like a warm hug. He noticed the cool calming air on his fur, the quiet hum of the meadow waking for the night, sleepy insects and rustling leaves, and the beautiful slow reveal of the starry sky. Not a wild rush of excitement, but a peaceful unfolding wonder, like watching a flower bloom in slow motion. He gave a contented little sigh. “You’re right, Lark. This is a beautiful kind of adventure. Waiting for the stars to come out.”

And so the little squirrel and the gentle lamb sat together in the quiet meadow, watching the sky blossom with light. The moonlight, spilling softly over the hills, warmed them like a silvery blanket, and the night sounds lulled them into perfect peace. Crispin’s busy paws finally stilled. Lark’s fleece was a comforting warm presence. The air smelled of damp earth and sweet night blooms. Soon his busy thoughts grew quiet, and her gentle breathing was the most peaceful sound he could hear. They were both very sleepy, ready to dream their own starry dreams, safe and sound as the world slumbered under the watchful eyes of the newly arrived stars.

Thus the shyest lights come out for those who wait, and notice.
